I was informed about the lay-off whilst out on sick leave (March 4), three days before I went into labor with my first baby (March 7). I gave birth on March 8. The deadline to sign the severance agreement was 7 March. My job role was officially terminated on 14 March. 

I found this timeline incredibly stressful and looking back on it with a clearer head, it seems ridiculous and unnecessary. I spent the those two days before labor very upset from the news and trying to speak to an employment lawyer (which was challenging given the timeline), and basically felt like I had no choice but to sign the contract knowing I could go into labor at any moment. My first week postpartum I spent doing admin, clearing my laptop and having 'goodbye chats' with people in my team as I knew my access to Bain systems would be cut off on Friday 14th. 

I cannot express how stressful the entire experience was, and it really tarnished those first days / weeks when I was supposed to be focusing on my health and my new baby. I feel like it would have been kinder to extend those deadlines to give me more time so I did not feel so rushed and pressured.

column117:
Unless Bain starts to review and penalize partners who sell understaffed/unreliable cases, our sustainability issues won't be solved. Bain doesn't have the right incentives to ensure sustainability and keep the teams energized. We are, currently, a slide factory, and not the company that claims to "Play for #1".

I started my career at Bain completely convinced that I would be a partner someday, but when I realized that was little (near to none) interest from the company to make it in a sustainable way, I lost the passion that I had about the company. My PD advisor was amazing, she was there to support me and give me the right directions, but my journey was absolutely unsustainable, and I had to choose between my health or my career. 

The level of demand in terms of commitment is absolutely unreliable and the market offers better experiences with similar financial value proposition. If Bain doesn't review it's way of working ASAP, we will keep loosing good consultants. 

Just as an example: I had a partner (Robin Bartling) laughing at me because I wasn't sleeping during the case (due to the amount of work I had to do). How should I respond to that?? My leadership laughing at my mental health? That was completely absurd. And as far as I know, this partner wasn't penalized for his behavior. Why does that still happens with no strong action to avoid such cases? This was just one example that happened to me, but South America offices have plenty of such cases, I believe every bainie has been through this, and this is unacceptable.

column117: 2nd-year ACs/Cs should be discouraged from joining PEG by staffing managers if they've never done PEG before. This is especially true for non-MBA hires at the Consultant level who are usually less better equipped for succeeding in PEG. PEG is a harsh enough environment that someone with that kind of tenure at Bain (2nd year AC/C) without prior PEG experience are at risk of getting crushed in terms of sustainability and performance reviews. Sure M's/SM's are instructed to go easier for the first few diligences, but the bars for performance are still there. C2s/SACs who have never done PEG before are being compared with C1s/AC2's who've only ever done PEG and it can be a recipe for disaster. I have personally heard about these types of comparisons being verbalized by LT and it's demoralizing. A suggested fix is to have requirements for a certain percent of each incoming glass required to do PEG. If it's that much of the business, then train up the talent to fill it rather than burning your tenured GP talent who you put into PEG later. That criticism aside, Bain was still a great place : )

column117:
When I was planning my return from my secondment I felt let down by Bain a few times which contributed to my decision to not return:
1) I emailed staffing / PD to ask to extend my secondment by 3 months. I did not receive a reply so sent a follow-up email which was also not responded to. I then asked my mentor to chase and after this I received a reply saying that would not be possible. 
2) I then replied to the above email asking for a staffing chat instead so that I could try and link my return project to my secondment. I received no reply to this email until about a month later when I had reached out to an SM to discuss roles in their practice area (see number 3).
3) I reached out to an SM to discuss roles in the CP practice area - an area of interest from my secondment. They responded very enthusiastically and replied suggesting a call. I replied with times available and received no response, instead I received a reply from staffing (to my email from a month previous) to set-up a staffing chat. 
4) In said staffing chat I was told the areas of interest I had previously mentioned / reached out to would not be possible as they are now 'flex' options and I couldn't do a back-to-back flex. These were not flex options before I left but I understand that things have changed in the past 6 months. The list of staffing options really did not inspire me and that was the tipping point in my decision to leave. 

Through this series of events I felt like Bain were not showing me the care and consideration I had previously attributed to the firm - Bain is a place I loved and felt loved - but through this process I felt like I was just another head needed to fill a row in an excel model. I know this will be due to headcount pressures etc. and really am not blaming any individual - I just really want there to be awareness that when headcount pressures drive these sort of actions it can actually exacerbate the issue.

column156:
Planning to combine clinic work with management consulting, as you know leaving for McKinsey, starting that role in October, balancing with ongoing clinic work. I had cross offers from McK and Bain way back in 2020, difficult decision to start with, a few key reasons tipped towards Bain, I felt Bain / got the impression it would be a bit more nurturing to come up to curve making a big transition in work. After having 2 tenure holds and not progressing at all and the way that was approached and handed, lost faith that I was fit to be successful at Bain or it was the right fit for me. Had one tenure hold in April, then 3 months later had another tenure hold. Never progressed in whole year, that was an issue to me in itself, demoralizing, destroyed confidence in myself and the system. lt could have been handled better, just didnâ€™t feel very transparent process. First one was kind of ok, second one really shocked, didnâ€™t see it coming. Thought I was addressing all the constructive feedback getting, overall was positive and had a few points that I was actively addressing. 

Was really shocked and when I looked into the reasons why it was hard to get an answer as to who decided this and why it happened. Manager couldnâ€™t explain. Communication lacked some sensitivity and empathy, was told it doesnâ€™t matter and told that repeatedly. Came from people in key roles where I felt there should have been some more transparency. Made me lose faith in the system. 

Didnâ€™t know anything about tenure system before I started. Until I heard people saying C1, didnâ€™t actually know how it worked. Didnâ€™t know about tenure system until it came up in conversations, no formal training on what happens with tenure, how itâ€™s assessed. Found out about adhoc. Steve did hold a meeting as class captain right before we were told tenure not progressing. But wasnâ€™t sure on the timing and the re-assessment of it, how it all works. Definitely some upfront messaging about it would have helped with expectations.

Messaging up front was donâ€™t worry, just get a feel for what a Bain case is and youâ€™ll have 6-12 months to settle in and no expectations of you. Just donâ€™t worry and learn. But when getting assessed every 3 months for tenure, there are still evaluations that are going on that effect you and also youâ€™re feeling of how doing in the role. 

3 possible alternatives to integrating industry conâ€™s / tenure system:
1. Had a lot of messaging at the start that Bain is not set up for industry consultants to be successful. Rather than waiting for people to have tenure holds and deal with consequences at that point, actively intervene and get feedback and flag e.g. you are not on track, hereâ€™s how you can address it and who is here to help you. More proactivity around this early on. Supporting people more in filling their gaps. That is the approach I would have preferred. 
2. Perhaps have a separate tenure system for industry conâ€™s, different skills tracker maybe or tenure. Not the same as promote-throughs. Feels like it should be different.
3. Have industry cons progress as usual, make the up ticks but a lower expectation from the LT. Not be told they are having a hold for the first 12 months. Avoids having confidence rocked. 
Tenure was the main driver for me on why I wanted to leave. 

Could of other things I wanted to feedback into four different areas: 
Second points around the healthcare opportunities in staffing. I knew coming in Bain didnâ€™t have a big healthcare practice, my assumption was even though less healthcare cases and less people interested e.g. much less doctors and people with healthcare background, so assumed I would be preference to be staffed on those as they came around. Was a discussion around having a healthcare ringfence regionally/globally, that would certainly help for retention and recruitment for people in healthcare. Wouldnâ€™t have been on any healthcare cases for 12 months if I didnâ€™t get on the last one. 

One more key point:
Think Bain is already looking at this, stage of life I am at, better policies for working mothers and people going through. Egg freezing and IVF benefits e.g. McK have better policies on this e.g. parental leave, cover cost of egg freezing, not sure if they cover upfront costs.

â€¢	Denmark; Head of Interaction Design

My ambition for ADAPT: Loved to see top three management consulting firms cracking problems utilizing human centricity. I really liked the ambition of Bain leadership at that time, which had innovative thinking. 
I was able to successfully apply my skillsets to cases, but thereâ€™s always a period of intense education and trying to structure the case team to work with ADAPT. Thatâ€™s where the gaps come from. Second gap is how to commercialize ADAPT. Bain Partners think of ADAPT as a vendor. For an Innovation case, there are times when we can only staff one Innovation Expert and designer. 
Third gap is a fair amount of leadership shift in ADAPT. It felt like we had a lot of support growing this capability within Bain without having to do acquisitions, which is McKinseyâ€™s strategy. Bainies are generally very open to everyoneâ€™s voice, and we have very inclusive culture. In consultancy side, thereâ€™s marks to be hit to perform well. When Experts come into a case team, the role is less clearly defined, itâ€™s hard to define the room for education of new ways of working. Weâ€™re really easily able to revert back to our ways of working. This has really improved in the last couple of years, but influence is still really important and it feels lacking from ADAPT sometimes. I loved my time at Bain, but I do think that the 6 month promotion cycle is detrimental to retaining talent, especially at the M --> SM level. If I had returned from leave and been staffed quickly to a case where I could have been up for promotion, I very likely would have stayed through the promotion period and at a minimum through my first year as an SM. It's very daunting to come back after a career break like parental leave, and I didn't feel there was any momentum in trying to get me back into the rhythm of the job.

I also think there should be an opportunity to provide more formal opportunities for mentorship to all Cs. I am an introverted person, and trying to build mentor relationships outside of my direct supervisors and PD advisors took me until my M year. I know that certain affinity groups provide formal matching and I understand there are a lot of Cs, but I think I would have benefited from feeling that someone more senior and farther along in the working parent journey had been invested in me earlier in my career at Bain.

column156:
Don't have a concrete job lined up yet, but exploring other personal projects with some friends; advising and participating in some start-ups; I would like to build something from scratch that I own. 

Consulting is an industry where you can see different clients/problems. Everything is new all the time and you can learn a lot, but you don't see things grow. You can't keep building on what you've accomplished before. I would like to be in a place where I can see things evolve in real time. 

Important for AIS to focus on: There currently isn't a career path for technical talent where the outcome does not lead to Expert Partner. It pushes people to have a more commercial oriented career, but it's not for everyone, especially with the type of Talent we have in AIS. We need to have an alternative where people can take on more responsibilities/senior roles that doesn't necessarily mean you have to be a Partner. 

Separately, the experience someone has within Bain depends a lot on on the project/client/Partner - there's a lot of variability. That's understandable in this industry, but the variability shouldn't be that high. There's people who have awful experiences, and other types of projects which are great. There should be guardrails where things don't go that badly - we need to have parameters in place.

Financially, this will be a lateral financial moveâ€”about total compensation of USD 580K, which is about a 10% boost to current comp. Iâ€™ll be joining at the Director level, which is two clicks below Partner. 

I&D has one signature SKU, which was new venture creation. Product let by Dennis Jones is really strong. In talking to some of those team members, it sounds like pricing/positioning is hard to do in the market, with BCG being more established and willing to take equity for payment from clients. That particular SKU never scaled. 

I also participated in the Engineering Excellence SKU with the ET practice. That one was tough, because it wasnâ€™t really an I&D SKU.

What I liked about I&D is that I could leverage the integrated team, help support work and be supported. 

What Iâ€™ve heard from my peers right now is that Vector is a doughnut, and the missing hole is the LT, or that Vector is a circular firing squad. Itâ€™s really not One Team within Vector. 

Bainâ€™s operating is based on partner interlock. Johnny did that for both ET and Global Eng. When we transitioned, my understanding is Johnny was shown the door, and there wasnâ€™t anyone else taking on that partner interlock for us going forward. 

We donâ€™t have time or opportunities to interface with senior partners. Most people that I talk to at the leadership level are indoctrinated AAG ways of working. It was a tough transition from servant leader model, previously managed by Eric Lee and Johnny Lee. Outside of Bain walls, Iâ€™d be proud to call both of them my boss. 

My day-to-day experience being managed by a non-technical person was very tough. I donâ€™t think the program manager model works for a technical group. The apprentice model is hard to maintain at the global level. Itâ€™s not like in general consulting, where they are tied to an office. For us, thereâ€™s no one at the office level able to help with a lot of the things I talked about. Weâ€™re a talent pool thatâ€™s not being integrated. 

I was hired into Bain to grow the digital business. I always expected that thereâ€™s pain associated with being part of a new part of the business. The question that people have to ask themselves is if they want to be a digital leader in a very conservative management consulting firm? I felt like when people hired me, I was clear on what trade-offs I was making.

Some of the trade-offs and pain points are that ase teams are not flexible to ways of working. When I was heavily involved in hiring and recruiting, I was pretty adamant to hire more senior folks so they know what theyâ€™re getting into, instead of people straight out of college. 

What Iâ€™ve appreciated is strong mentorship from Johnny when he was here. Chris Brahm made it clear that we were purposely investing in groups like AAG. The messaging was clear is that we trying to grow, and weâ€™re trying to figure it out, so please be patient with us. With the hiring spree recently, I never really understand that. We were outgrowing the demand. No investment in a solution or a strategy, but it was like we were hiring more delivery team members and not more senior partners. Now that looks like Iâ€™m competing with these folks for staffing assignments, instead of  working together to create new growth initiatives. 

When you feel like BCG is opposition for Bain in anything, Bain should at least be following the leader, since theyâ€™re more well-established.

I also had to repay my MBA and for this I had a crazy experience - I got sponsored by Bain Italy to go to IE Business School. The contract stated that I had to stay 2 years with Bain after the mba and if I left I would have had to repay the full amount. After 1y and 1 month, I transferred to Bain London. Then, Bain Italy asked Bain London to pay the full amount of the MBA. Therefore, Bain London asked me to stay additional 2 years with the condition that if I leave Bain before 1 year I had to pay the total MBA amount (and this is what happened).

However, I discovered that the MBA policy repayment for Bain London is a sliding scale from day 1 when you come back from your mba and it has not been applied to me. Additionally, when I communicated that I would have left, finance told me that I had 3 months to pay everything (and I never signed anywhere for this deadline!!!!). I think that it's crazy that there are so different policy around MBA among offices of the same region and I think I received a very unfair treatment (both from Bain Italy and from Bain London). 
For the future, I would really recommend that you work on the harmonization of mba policies around offices.
Thank you,
Joseph Bonomo

column117: Bain SF office is very diverse and hence requires more training at the leadership level to understand and deal with diversity. For example, one of the interns I was working with had a disability related to reading and listening, I didn't know how to deal with it and reaching out for help didn't work out either. I ended up googling and training myself. What was worse was that the immediate leadership was dismissive of it stating something to the effect of: this disability won't work in a fast paced consulting world. The LT, especially home grown / young leaders need to be exposed to the outside world so the culture can be more balanced. That is one reason I am also leaving Bain because I am sure there is value in having a diverse set of experiences to be a global leader. Many people who have only lived or worked in the US, and within, only in SF don't even understand (forget sympathizing or empathizing) what challenges things like immigration, visa processing, overseas travel, falling sick in a new country, but having gone to school in the US, not understanding the cultural references when playing games bring. Immigrants and even people who aren't SF natives aren't often able to connect, and will never be able to at that level, and it is on the shoulders of the leadership to be responsible. For example, I am from India and one of the C2s on my team mocked India in front of the entire team when talking to the AP. The AP laughed at moved ahead, which was appalling to me to such an extent that I didn't even want to fight it back. I want to emphasize that most Bainies have the right mindset, the home growns need to be trained better, especially those who don't go to B School and hence haven't had outside exposure, especially that of a flat hierarchy and diversity. However, even those that have the right mindset might not behave like a true global leader because they don't have the right experiences or exposure, and that is where trainings become really important.

In my case, this issue became most acute in my last case. What made the experience difficult was not the final outcome itself, but the way the transition was handled: I experienced limited transparency, a rapid loss of support locally, and a disconnect between the support that had initially been signaled and what was actually provided in practice. That was disappointing and had a meaningful impact on how I experienced the end of my time at Bain.

Once the departure path was clearly defined, the process became much more workable. Earlier directness and more consistent support would have made the experience feel more respectful and better managed.

column156:
As you think about your upcoming departure from Bain, what are your plans (b-school, new role, etc.) and what do you hope to accomplish?

Next role will be working as generalist consultant at McKinsey. Wanted to join Bain as an Expert as a differentiator to my career, but after a year, I wanted to learn the project management and team communication side of things. At this phase in my career, I want to learn more about business-solving skills and become a project manager, so I can do projects in other industry. 

I originally wanted to join general consulting within Bain, but one of my peers in the Seoul office did not get an offer after going through the general consulting interview process, so I applied for a role at McKinsey. 

I talked to a lot of AAG leaders about what we need to do differently in APAC to be more integrated with general consulting AAG needs to be more integrated into the team, and not acting as support services. AAG needs to have the mindset that they are able to serve as consultants. Right now, AAG is not staffed on the entirety of a case in the Seoul office and other APAC offices. Sometimes this is a business decision or due to budget. However, if you really want to maximize using AAG members, you need to engage them from the beginning to the end of the project. I understand it could be a staffing issue. In a more mature office like Australia, I was able to see instances where AAG was staffed for the entire case, and it worked really well. However, this concept is not as developed in other APAC offices. I did two cases with Seoul, one that worked really well and another who didnâ€™t work as well. In the latter type of case, thereâ€™s a time crunch for data scientists to prepare things because AAG did not have a chance to give input on how much time a deliverable required. 

The Seoul office is very successful with it comes to general consulting and supporting its consultants. Seoul LT doesnâ€™t have much experience with working with AAG.. There needs to be examples of good embedded cases; GC needs to be open to changing their working style in order to incorporate specialists. There should be a new working model in Bain. 

I have had instances where I felt undervaluedâ€”we had a demanding client and had to put something together in a quick timeline. I didnâ€™t have the time to pull something together due to different expectations with the case manager. My AAG Sr Manager was able to negotiate the timeline and give us more time, and helped me prove that we could do our best out of three days we negotiated. 

Instances where I felt valued: My first case working with Australia client, and whenever I brough insights to the project manager, I felt like my work was valued and was the basis of the case teamâ€™s answer.

The outplacement support opportunities should be significantly improved, as they are currently almost non-existent. I had informal discussions with 3 partners I knew well during my time at Bain, but these conversations did not result in any support regarding potential exit opportunities, introductions, or networking contacts to explore future roles.

For a firm such as Bain, this is a critical area to strengthen. Supporting departing talent in transitioning into key organizations and leadership roles can also help build long-term relationships with future clients and stakeholders. Leaving individuals entirely responsible for identifying and securing their own exit opportunities weakens the relationship between Bain and departing employees, ultimately reducing the likelihood that alumni will engage Bain again for future support or business opportunities.

Based on my experience and discussions with peers, both BCG and McKinsey provide materially stronger support in this area (e.g. they provide with 2/3 exit opportunities and/or networking contacts to explore)

In addition, this is now the third time I have been asked to provide the same departure information (e.g., personal email address):

* First on Workday before leaving;
* Second through the departure form sent by email to the local office (including guardian selection);
* Third through this form (including guardian selection again).

Despite repeatedly providing the same contact details, the survey link was ultimately sent to an email address different from the one communicated in all previous departure forms. This reflects a lack of coordination in the offboarding process and creates unnecessary friction during departure.

There's one side of the spectrum that is pure technical experts and another side where a full case team could be completely made up of AIS doing client management; you have a very diverse group of people. What gets people out of bed sometimes is learning new things, then you have people who want to be in front of clients; it's a broad spectrum. We've talked about this sort of technical track, if you want to retain people, that might be good at what they do, but may not make it to the next promotion, if they have to do GC work, 

Even APT last year, the language was still that AIS is back-end. 

Besides the first three months at Bain, I've staffed myself on project. I don't think we do enough of that at the C/M level. I encourage my advisees to build that network for themselves. Selling may always sounds scary, but it is just being upfront and realistic about what you are capable of, and what the business is capable of.

column117:
More feedback for the office:

- In general I had a great experience at Bain, and I think the Dubai office is improving in terms of sustainability. However there are a few things I want to call out that I think can help the firm/ office in the future
- Regarding sustainability, I think we need to be a bit more analytical in out approach. Really sustainability will just be determined by the volume of work divided by the number of qualified people on a case. We need to focus on adjusting those metrics going forward if we really want to fix it.
- The onus is still usually on the junior team to push for sustainability in cases, and when you have a major power imbalance (i.e. all new juniors) it's very hard to do this. We need official HR policies around things like dinner breaks in the WFH context.
- Reviews are still pretty subjective, and the problem is worse when every manager has to give a review, even when they've only seen a couple weeks of work (i.e. an ongoing case before a review cycle). I got a really frustrating review in that situation (case I had only been on for 3 weeks before a review cycle), where the manager gave a flat SC with no check-ups which I know did not reflect my performance and in the end took me down from an FE to an SC for the cycle. 

In the end I think it's more helpful to give constructive feedback, obviously the people and the culture are wonderful at Bain apart from the sustainability. I would 100% do it all again and would love the chance to work with Bain teams in the future from the client side. Cheers!

column117: Bain should concede search time to voluntary leaves - currently not happening in the Madrid office (or only to some people). I was conceded 0 search time after 5 years at Bain, with a performance of always "Strong" and "Frequently Exceeding" Expectations, and a fast track promotion. People who get let go (because they are underperforming, on PIIP plans etc) receive 4 months of search time, while people who have always performed, succeeded and gave it all get 0 search time. This situation seems unfair to me and I believe it is not aligned with Bain's interests (after all, me being in a good position post Bain could benefit Bain in the future). Also, I believe it creates an incentive to underperform to employees who think of leaving. From my knowledge, competitors also give search time to voluntary leaves (e.g. MCK in Portugal). I think Bain should rething this for the future and align with peers.

column156:
It's a weird feeling, almost 19 years at Bain with many good friendships. It is bittersweet to a professional end of those relationships. It's good to hear that we've done something right back when we had the AAG team. I've talked to many individuals that say if they had to define their perfect job profile, it would have been AAG 5-7 years back. We really had a team back then that stuck together; we defined our strategy and this was done together. While we felt the second class citizenship even more back in the day, we still had a better time than now, and NPS score of 70+ back in old AAG. That doesn't mean we should go back to that, I really think we should stay in the direction we are now. But the next step that AIS is independently running more of the particular tech workstream in lieu of consultants, which may not be as efficient in the current set-up. This requires a big step up for our team members to work on communication skills, and not every individual has those skills. 

From my career perspective, I probably made some mistakes when we set up the guilds. I was always delivering production, and the distinction to be in DSMLE was to be a super-coder, which did not feel like my profile. But that led me to be put in the Expert program, so I slowly moved out of guild responsibilities. I was successful in my cases and was continuing as an individual contributor. I currently have no additional responsibilities, which is a bit strange given my tenure. 

Critique of Florian Mueller - we don't fit to each other. It's a non-relationsihp, this was also visible when I handed in my resignation. The insurance practice tried to get me on partner promotion to retain me. They said they reached out to AIS practice, the answer was negative without a further comment. Only one person did not react to my resignation, which is Florian. Finally I asked his EA to schedule time, so we had a short meeting, which was 10 minutes where we ran out of things to say to each other. This was good confirmation of my decision to leave. He didn't even say hello to me at the Munich training. He also does this to case teams. We had a case from last Nov to May, and he didn't greet to the case teams. Consultants say that he never says hello or thank you. This is unacceptable. He's very successful in selling cases, so there is a strong justification for why he is in his job. But as a leader, that is unacceptable. 

The intervews for my new role already started in the beginning of June. The interviews were not just interviews but nice conversations, but the probability that I will leave  Bain was very high by then. It's a new start for me, I can learn from my mistakes, and am going to focus on relationship building internally and externally. I got the impression during the conversations that there was proper team culture. It is going to be in the direction that I suggested, they run their own workstreams which are sold together with industry partners. Roadmap and criteria to Partner are much clearer, a strong feeling of support.

Next step: not sure might be more tech or start up focused

column117:
Bain's commitment to providing opportunities and resources to consulting staff is world-class. The culture and environment for both consulting staff and business functions are generally similar (supportive, opportunities for development, great people, etc.). However, the way Bain internally talks about Business Function can feel, at times, demeaning and exclusive. It often feels like the business is talked about in a way that is "consultants" and then "everyone else"; in the "everyone else" bucket exists every spectrum of capability from AAG to Recruiting to Assistants to PPK to Digital - our capabilities and what we each bring to the table often feels overlooked in one brush stroke. In terms of solutions, simple language shifts from 'case team' to 'team' feel immediately implementable. Similarly, when an initiative is being rolled out, a Business Function member (not a former consultant turned Business Function) should be on the committee to encourage inclusion given Business Function members make up a huge portion of Bain.

On a more personal note, I believe (and hope) my Business Function experience in managing is not the 'norm', but I had a terrible managing experience. While my supervisor was supportive, available, and empathetic, I felt so isolated, ill equipped, and untrained - I shouldn't have been managing individuals without prior manager training, I had no idea who to reach out to when I felt my manager was equally (if not more so) under water, and I had no voice in the hiring decisions of who I would be managing. My 'training on the job' was emotionally and physically taxing, and I felt I could emotionally combust at any given moment. The isolation I felt reflected the perceived lack of resources I had as a Business Function member - while there may have been resources for me, I didn't know where to begin in asking for them. In terms of solutions, I recommend equipping leadership team members with trainings for aspiring managers.

All in all, Bain is a fantastic place that I felt lucky to be a part of!

Not related to the departure process but wanted to share some additional feedback on my time at Bain.

As mentioned, during my three year tenure I speak for myself and peers when I say we were constantly living in fear and stress over if we were meeting expectations. I put my personal life on pause in order to do the job, which was highly unsustainable even without a family. I regularly felt undervalued. In order to be a 'Best place to work' I would challenge Bain to have employees (below SM) who are able to maintain some degree of work life balance - be an involved parent that does not depend on a stay at home spouse or extended family nearby, or exercise regularly and eat healthy. I saw no examples of this during my time. Due to my experience at Bain I began therapy and took mental health leave. I would encourage Bain to have a more direct feedback culture and openly talk about performance improvement plans. I often felt I received feedback on my work or case but did not receive direct feedback on long term trajectory, despite asking for it, which is detrimental after working extremely hard and putting in long hours at an intense job. 

I would challenge Bain to set more boundaries and establish more consistency on hours and action feedback that teams voice instead of strictly listening. People consistently worked weekends without telling their manager or SMAP in order to meet deadlines which was not sustainable but set expectations for speed and quality of output for broader Bain. Lastly, balancing extra 10s and recruiting on top of case work consistently felt unachievable, adding to unsustainability.

column117:
Cutting people two weeks before the holidays was extremely bad. Would've preferred first week of January or November. The month is so full of family, business, and a recharging which was mostly erased managing this. 

The off boarding is missing an employee specific list that's on ONE PAGE (not 40page pdf) with an succinct list  of their possible benefits extended, key dates for those, actions required, and key contacts for those. Having overview one sheets for complex parts of things is so useful to someone under stress trying to figure out what's next. Getting a 40 page pdf to try to balance the emotional swings and reading through pages of info looking for an amalgamation of this is an agitator and risk area for not getting things done in the right cadence, sequence, and priority. Absent of this one sheet - it creates a more, not less, vunerable state for the departing employee.

Having a one sheet on communication. Clearly there was a script on the HR/leadership side, so these points exist - but were told (not shown or typed) for the end user. Being shared this information on the initial call is like telling critical information to someone being inundated with white noise. The shock of the moment is in no way able to also capture critical information. Having a one sheet leave behind of what the team knows, what I can can communicate when and how, who can I expect to have contact with, helps the exiting employee know what they can and can't ask for to maintain a professional communication line with their exiting. I wasn't clear who I could talk to and about what - and can I contact my old boss or not? Communication was quickly funneled to my HR contact and was given the impression that's how it had to stay. I felt uncomfortable asking for this - not sure why - probably because when my boss stopped communicating about a topic and HR took over - without explanation - it felt odd and cold. Knowing why would've helped. 

Not having my direct manager lay me off was odd, and not sure why. While I appreciate having her boss do it - or anyone (as it's a very tough thing to do) - not sure why the person who was making this decision that I should be terminated, didn't have to do this to me. Felt cold and lacked accountability. 

Caitlin Fallon is a hero - a true Bainie and human who balanced both sides of my off boarding. Holding the balance of Bain's needs and our concerns is not easy and takes great skill. Truly appreciated her - especially when hearing she was balancing her own imminent arrival of a new child. Selfless and kind. Meant everything to my family.

Overall, I leave Bain as a strong promoter, given the experiences I gained, the learning opportunities I received, and the people I worked with. That said, a few elements materially worsened my departure experience and affected my perception of how the firm values those who are leaving.

1. PD cycle exclusion for departing employees
I find it difficult to understand why individuals immediately fall out of the PD cycle once they announce their departure. This results in no further reviews, no continued engagement in PD discussions, and no recognition through the performance bonus above the 100% cap. In practice, this means that people who mentally â€œlog offâ€ are rewarded the same as those who continue to deliver for their teams until the very last day. The logic feels misaligned, especially in periods of high workload, where incentives for strong performance by departing colleagues would be even more important.

2. Case experience in recent months
Over the past months in DACH, case teams were visibly overstretched. Despite this, commercial considerations repeatedly outweighed team sustainability. For the first time in my 4.5 years at Bain, I had the impression that senior leadership did not sufficiently prioritize the well-being of case teams, instead pushing until people were at their limits. Leaving with this impression was disappointing, particularly in a firm that places such strong emphasis on culture.

You need to create and manage an appeals process by which Bainies who believe they have been wrongly forced onto transition may make a case and have their case heard.  I feel very strongly that I was wrongfully pushed out, but without an appeals process within Bain, and having been required to sign away my rights to receive severance, Bain has unwittingly forced one of their greatest advocates and promoters to leave the firm even as others sit and seek to only work the bare minimum while eyeing the right startup to leave toward.

Also - I was informed that I would be forced onto transition 6 days after the end of open enrollment.  What that means is that I elected to put a bunch of money into my FSA under the assumption that I would be getting surgery and continuing at Bain during 2023.  Because of the end of open enrollment, I was not able to change that election, and now I will lose close to a thousand dollars in FSA deductions into thin air.  That's really bad.  You need to make sure that people that you are pushing out around the time of open enrollment are informed of that BEFORE they have to make these kinds of decisions that will cause them to lose money if they are not informed.

Within Aura, things are actually going very well from a business perspective. I joined Baincubator and Aura from the very beginning. With an entrepreneurial spirit, I was looking for Aura to be able to make the next step; a lot of things that made me leave could have been overlooked if the company was ready for the next step. 
A lot of the questions that are being asked now are ones that are being asked from the very beginning of Aura. The market comp piece was also important. The trouble with Baincubator is that career progression is always put on hold or not a priority, because leaders are waiting to see if weâ€™re spinning this out. Rest of my peers in general consulting are senior managers at this point. Locked progression with the lack of uncertainty, which is ironic with the amount of independence you want to have as an entrepreneur.  	
Entity formation and issuance is always a big questio;; entrepreneurs are always one foot in or one foot out about this. Everyone wanted to do equity issuance, but itâ€™s a very foreign thing for Bain because it is precedence setting. The mentality was like that we should let this play out to a further stage and then make a decision, but the battle that you now have to face is that thereâ€™s a tax liability. Well, if you had incorporated earlier, then everyone gets a tax bill for where that lands. Itâ€™s easy for the entrepreneurs to think that this is Bainâ€™s fault for not setting up early. It feels like everyone else got guinea-pigged in. It would be a shame if the next cohort if Bain didnâ€™t learn from the experience. 
Expectations for Baincubator/Aura played out the way I expected. Coming in, with innovation at Bain; innovation is a slight asterisk. You know what the inefficiencies are going to be. If anything, there should be an unconditioning camp for general consultants that want to join the Baincubator. For a lot of people, like me and my cofounders, you want to run a lot of presentations and make a lot of slides. If you want to continue to staff from the core, you need to break some habits from the consulting world. Even coming in with the mentality of corporate innovation; thereâ€™s not a lot of downside (no concept of a burn), there was an oscillation between making a safe bet vs. making a decision that was riskier but could have significantly more upside. 
Most of our gains all came from training entrepreneurs â€“ giving them a taste of success. Thatâ€™s probably the key to building the next cohort. You canâ€™t downplay the value of iterating on something small. 
People management: If weâ€™re not able to get to the point of establishing C corps and equity, we need to make sure incentives are aligned are gross margin sharing to keep people motivated once they realize Aura is already outperforming a general practice team, but weâ€™re not being compensated at that level The other thing that needs to be fixed is what finance structure. The way that we have done it so far is that weâ€™re only being viewed as a cost center and not a revenue generator. We had to fight for that spend when weâ€™re being treated as a cost center.

During my departure process I was informed by BCA that generally, I should only reach LT members with specific leads in mind (e.g. a specific opportunity for a company that I know that partner is involved with). So more of a targeted approach.

Thus, when it comes to the Bain network, I was relying on my mentor to help me with a more exploratory approach and open the channels within Bain. That did not happen as my mentor did not keep the contact going with me since Jan/Feb 2024, despite some attempts  from my side. So we never had sessions to help me finding another opportunity.

So essentially I felt like I was on my own.

But now in mid June 2024, I received contact from a key member from the staffing / Hr / development team, and we started an initiative involving the local office LT to discuss opportunities. I am in the process of scheduling the first chats with each one. I am really hoping this will allow me to leverage their network and potentially yield results.

While this recent initiative is definitely welcome and I hope this will prove useful, the reality is that precious time was lost on this process.

So my feedback would be for the different parts to keep a tighter control loop especially when it comes to cases involving transition to ensure that the employee leaving has an adequate support from Bain in transitioning to the next opportunity in their career.

column117:
During my experience at Bain South Africa, I observed that the company values its workforce, but not necessarily it's people as there are inconsistencies in how individuals are treated. For example, I encountered instances of miscommunication and unfair treatment, specifically during my time on DNA, such as a supervisor providing misleading feedback on my performance for three months and having a review approved without sufficient evidence, with only one example provided for six remedial development areas. Additionally, I experienced a change in supervisors during my last month on a case, which led to a review written by someone who had worked with me for less than a month. My first supervisor, who had worked with me for the majority of the time, did not contribute to my review but provided detailed feedback for another colleague, covering each metric of the skills tracker for her. In a discussion with my first supervisor about the remedial development opportunities, some feedback lacked supporting evidence or examples. Numerous challenges were associated with the DNA case, including issues related to structuring, lack of clear direction, and general uncertainty regarding the tasks at hand. These difficulties were not solely a reflection of my performance, but rather indicative of broader problems within the case that affected the overall work process.

Although I passed a PI, there is no guarantee that such issues will not occur again. I initially believed that Bain would value me as an individual and my contributions, but this expectation has not been met. My performance on my previous case, where I worked directly with a partner and was given a positive review, was not taken into consideration when evaluating my improvement. Despite receiving a 3 rating on the next case review after the DNA case, I still had to undergo PI for H1, which is inconsistent with my demonstrated improvement. Performance ratings appear subjective and are the primary basis for judgment, which may not accurately reflect an individual's overall capabilities and growth.

The PD process at Bain is unclear, as evidenced by multiple instances of conflicting information. One example of such confusion is regarding the possibility of a PEG case being assigned for PI. Initially, I was informed that PEG would not be an option for PI, only to be later told by a partner that a PEG case would indeed be assigned for my PI. When inquiring about the supervisor's capacity on the PEG case to support my PI, I was assured that they had confirmed their availability. However, a few days later, I was informed that I could not be placed on PEG due to the supervisor's lack of capacity. This inconsistency highlights the need for improved clarity and communication within the PD process.

It was a HUGE shock for me that I was sacked. 
No warnings. No suggestions on how should do things differently. No advise.
I think that my team leader didn't want to spent time on me and on my development. Maybe I was  consider a thorn in the eye instead of an asset.
She took the easy way you might say.
What hit my hardest is that I was offered a leaving-package by HR, if that was what I wanted. I asked if I should consider this as an ultimatum. No! Not at all I was told. Not at all. It was an offer in case I was having thoughts on e.g. education or new career plans. 14 Days later the same HR person was there to sack me.
There had been no complaints. I hadn't violated business codes or behaviour codes. I did my job, even though I didn't feel that I was good at it.
I LOVED being in Bain. I was so proud being a little part of it and for what I did. I have gained friends from all teams from partners and down. Friends fo life. I am VERY GRATEFUL for my time, but very sad of my exit.
But I will never be open and honest to a team leader again. Your job will be on the line by doing so.

I had a brief discussion with my Sr. Director, Misha Bhan (HRBP), regarding my concerns related to my manager and my overall experience during the recent performance evaluation process.

The expectations from my role were only clearly communicated to me during the final performance evaluation, rather than through consistent guidance and feedback over time. During our conversation, when I mentioned that I was considering putting down my papers, he smirked, which I found quite disheartening after dedicating five years of hard work and commitment to Bain.

What I found most challenging was the lack of structured coaching or mentorship at a time when there was a perception that my performance was being impacted by circumstances. I believe earlier support, clearer guidance, and developmental conversations could have made a meaningful difference.

Additionally, the feedback shared by my last two managers, Rajni (ex-Bainie) and Tushar, often felt one-sided and lacked specific examples or balanced perspectives. When I attempted to provide context or explain my side of the situation, it did not feel like there was adequate openness to understanding the full picture.

I also observed a leadership style that, in my view, created divisions within the team rather than fostering collaboration. Over time, this led to visible strain in relationships among team members who were previously closely aligned and worked well together.

column117:
When I entered Bain, all the recruiters (consultants, managers, partners and HR) communicated me that Bain was a truly global firm, where I had the option to transfer wherever I wanted to and be part of an international community. My career was strong and Bain supported me to come to pursue an MBA at MIT Sloan, which I was very thankful for. For personal reasons (my boyfriend lives in NY) I decided to ask for a transfer to Bain US. The transfer process was very painful and I never felt supported by anybody, specially HR, which managed a very informal process. 

I saw how my classmates from BCG and McKinsey managed to transfer from international offices to the US smoothly. But it was not the case for any Bainee from South America (and also other countries). This is why I decided to apply to McKinsey NY, a place where I can continue my consulting career and a place where I have constantly seen how supportive they have been with all their employees, a truly global firm. I needed to be sure that the place I would work for would offer me that support, not only now, but for the future because I see my career in consulting. 

I really saw my future career at Bain because I love consulting and I was happy working there, amazing projects and amazing people. But now, I leave very sad. Sad because of the lack of support and clarity, because how Bain sold me a value proposition that did not meet when I really needed to. 

I hope my case can change the future of Bain South America, either by opening the door to future MBAs or by giving more clarity of the real value that Bain can offer to its employees.

Francisca Larraguibel

One of the biggest challenges AIS currently has in Tokyo is not having a say in casework. From what Iâ€™ve observed, experts get called into casework when their core expertise is absolutely needed. Itâ€™s like a part-time job and you donâ€™t have a say of how you can contribute to the client. Thereâ€™s no autonomy and control of what experts can do. There have been instances where things would have gone better on the case if the client could have visibility ahead of time of what expert consulting could achieve. Partners get billed for the work of AIS, so they have inherent incentive to minimize the hours allocated to experts. So with limited time, AIS is pulled in later. We get treated like part-timers. If that can be mitigated, AIS could contribute better, and we could have a say in strategic decisions.

I wish it was easier / more acceptable to reach out for career advice and support with plotting a route out of Bain. Until I received my departure materials, I didn't know how to access BCA or the Alum job board and there was no easy way for me to ask without going through staffing and PD, both of whom have influence over my prospects at Bain. As someone who's given a lot to the business, frequently exceeding / consistently outperforming, I was really disappointed in the leaving bonus. The fact that it doesn't take into account any outperformance and then also applies a 50% reduction, makes the whole thing feel very punitive and has left me feeling that Bain didn't really value my contribution. I tried to speak to Payroll about it but was given no support - my emails were ignored. I recognise that you can't simply get a pro-rated amount, but its worth thinking about how to make it feel more like a thank you (e.g. factoring in some kind of personal performance, or adjusting the 50% for outperformers). Its such a stark contrast to the rest of the departure process which makes you feel supported and a valuable member of the alum community.

After over three years of experience in high-pressure environments at Monitor Deloitte, I joined Bain & Company with the ambition to continue growing and contributing meaningfully. Unfortunately, I was placed in a project context that turned out to be professionally and psychologically toxic, primarily due to the conduct of a manager who failed to demonstrate the standards of leadership, respect, and collaboration that I believe should define any high-performance workplace like Bain. 

Despite my extreme willingness and commitment to contribute and operate at pace, I faced a pattern of micromanagement, undermining comments, and behavior that consistently eroded my ability to work with autonomy and confidence. On multiple occasions, I was publicly belittled for minor mistakes and, more disturbingly, I was subject to a remark related to my background and origins, which had no place in any professional setting.

A particularly serious episode where, following an internal error not attributable to me, I was made a scapegoat for a mistake in data handling. An incident I was not responsible for and for which I was not even allowed to explain my side. This led to my abrupt removal from the project, without due process or fair treatment, and ultimately led me to look for other job opportunities and resign from the company altogether after only a few months.

I choose to speak up about this experience not out of resentment, but because I believe itâ€™s essential to call out behavior that compromises the mental health and dignity of others, especially in environments that pride themselves on excellence and culture.

Going forward, I remain committed to building and supporting workplaces where integrity, mutual respect, and psychological safety are truly lived values.

column156:
I will go back to rejoin the company I was in before joining Bain. Effectively similar to old role in leading Data Science team, exciting part is that I'll be working with old colleagues who have developed themselves. It will be a challenge to reignite the relationship, but one that I look forward to. What I've learned from Bain is that I should be in the driver's seat of my own career goals. There was something in the past, that felt like was hard for me to achieve at that company. After being at Bain, I see that as long as I have a strong argument I can drive the outcome.

New role will be more product focused - we have a team of 20+ people, and, while there will be more than just 1-2 products, this is because the scope is bigger and we're developing long term goals. 

Case team/staffing: This is a challenge vs. what I see in general consulting. Everyone in AIS has the technical capacity, but they have different focuses. Even though we have discussed with the client what we are working on, it's not clear what skillset is needed to accomplish that. Sometimes it takes a few weeks for us to figure out that the team we have is not directly focused on what the right skillset is. It's hard to gauge from a staffing perspective what type of skills are needed. Scope creep is still an issue. We staff two people to do the work of three people. Given the amount of work and number of resources, you have one shot to get things right. This leads to people working long hours. From what I've heard, it sounds like a recurrent issue. 

How Bain can help people develop their careers: I see many members that seem to be stuck in their level, and I'm not sure if there's a concrete career path in achieving promotion to the next level. Naturally, after one or two rounds of promotions not happening, their motivations don't stay up. I think there are many good people at Bain that need a mentor. Mentorship mentality is strong on GC side, but not as strong in AIS. In industry, there's a clear reporting line and ownership. In the past two years, we've had a hiring freeze, so haven't had recruitment. I also haven't had a PD advisee. You can get very good people at different levels, I think the challenge once you get good and smart people, how do you integrate them into the team? From what I see, people are trying to use the people as a tool, but not investing in a way to develop them.

Josh's job search process has primarily consisted of connecting with the Global Coaching team and having chats with members of his network, including active and former Bainies. Josh is looking for a role in non profit or foundation work or in a for profit socially driven organization. Josh has a clear idea of the next role he would like and is choosing to wait for that opportunity vs taking what is available. Josh did note that for roles in non profit or not the norm of what Bainies typically go on to pursue beyond Bain, the job portal is not helpful.
Going to Rubric, over the next few years wants to go into operative role and wants to own something and see it evolve. Will see if it's something he wants to go towards.

My new role will be as a Senior Director (equivalent to Expert AP) at Simon-Kucher. The pay is significantly better, plus I will be in a consultant position. The bonus is also higher and it's a guaranteed path to Partner in three years if I am in good standing. Similar to Expert Consulting at Bain. 

In order for AIS to succeed, we should focus on the people. When I joined, we were < 100 people. We were a small team and very family-like. Of course this changes with team size, but we should strive to keep that environment as close to being a family as possible. I heard that there were rumors for an international team meeting, which is very promising. These days, many of the decisions for changes, like promotion process for example, are shared with delivery team members only at the very last minute. For many people, even at the junior level, it would good to inform them further in advance and walk through the thinking that guided the decision-making process. 

I don't think the guilds make sense as they are. It's unclear why we are separated into certain guilds, when staffing is reflective of what people specialize in and what they're interested in. The guild structure is only on paper. I think that's a good thing, but I wonder why we need guilds. 

Other ways of improving people culture would be having LT interact more with the delivery team, activities with full teams and trainings that all can attend together. 

We're hiring the right people. There were times when it felt like we were lacking juniors. The onboarding process is now very smooth.

These types of mistakes cannot happen, I was expecting that payment, was affected by not receiving it, and I still have the feeling I earned and deserved it. The process should include clearly written documents with "what you gain" and "what you lose", when signing the transition agreement. The agreement itself as a document, is also not clear enough as to these compensation topics.

column117:
Training, support, and mentorship needs to be more robust for early ACs at Bain NY. In addition, clarity on all expectations for an individual's tenure needs to be more thoroughly communicated during a person's beginning months at Bain. This can look like more company wide training sessions, more transparent communication about the review process, honest communication about team dynamics and norms, and tips on how to be a top performer at Bain & Company. Many ACs or individuals that have not been at Bain NY for long, feel like they had to swim in deep water during their first year to year and a half because they had to navigate unspoken rules within their Bain teams and did not feel adequately supported when completing tasks or receiving feedback. This is an issue because this leads to anxiety, stress, slowed employee development, and worse feedback. This can then negatively affect an individual's confidence and performance and can lead them into very difficult situations that feel insurmountable like performance watch, multiple gaps, or series of negative feedback.

Also, there needs to be better and more support for people of color at Bain NY. Bain NY talks a lot about how they have improved their recruiting channels to bring in more people of color and that is proven true based on the DEI data that Bain has shown over the past 2 years. But the issue is that Bain NY does not have the infrastructure to keep and develop its people of color. People of color and other folks at Bain may not write their dissatisfaction with Bain and its services on surveys that are talked about during class check-ins or other forums, but the dissatisfaction is very real and very present. I hope in the future that Bain NY can implement a system or infrastructure that offers better support to people of color. This can come in the form of mini groups that are composed of one person from consulting leadership and 3-4 people of color in early AC or consultant tenures. These groups can meet bi-weekly or monthly and need to finally create that safe space feeling where people can speak about the real issues they deal with at Bain. In addition, it would be extremely beneficial if these small groups introduce different trainings that span excel, mekko graphics, team communication norms, etc. If these small groups can create a safe space for people of color to talk about their issues and receive more training that can help them improve their performance, I believe there will be a dramatic shift in how people of color feel about Bain NY and how they perform in their teams. A different model would have to be used to address Bain NY or Bain & Company at large but I think an increased number of trainings that tackle excel, mekko graphics, client calls, team communication norms, etc, and having more forums like surveys or conversations that open up the floor for people to address what they deal with at Bain can improve how Bainies feel about Bain NY and Bain at large. If Bain & Company was a firm that did not claim to have one of the best corporate cultures, have employees who say they work with some of the best, friendly, and most interesting people, and made statements about how it truly cares about the success and well-being of its workers, I would not suggest any of these improvements. But I believe it is Bain's responsibility to bring about these changes and that these changes are completely within Bain's capabilities. Bain says that its culture is open and honest and that Bain will never let another Bainie fail. In my experience, the communication was open but not transparent and including of all detail; and the support was lacking and left me feeling like Bain was more interested in getting rid of me and picking at flaws that were already resolved, instead of wanting to keep me.

Bain has the opportunity to live up to the statements and claims it makes about itself. But I find it very disheartening and upsetting when statements like, "Man, I drank the kool-aid" or "People here are fake" are frequently heard in a place that talks about being so great, accommodating, and supportive. Bain does have great people and a want to be the best it can, but it has a large amount of work to do until people feel like they truly belong at Bain and weren't blinded by some type of kool-aid when they joined. I hope that Bain NY's culture continues to improve and that people feel more welcomed and secure, and do not feel that they need to constantly look over their shoulder when it comes to their performance. Please take this feedback to heart and implement it because Bain has the opportunity to be a place that truly has one of the best corporate cultures and have employees that genuinely feel and believe that it does.

The news about the lay-offs was a big shock, felt like we were going from zero to sixty. 
Primary Research is in a place where we need to reset or rebuild trust. It came as a surprise to all of us. Maybe that was a good thing, that leadership wasnâ€™t treating it as an issue until it became an issue. But the messaging feels off when it comes to the Vector re-org. After speaking to Gladys [Walter] and Dawn Kix, the timing is way too coincidental to not be related to the re-org. We were already going to be the smaller team going into Innovation & Design, and now thatâ€™s definitely true. 

AAG used to be its own separate thing and then became the delivery arm for advanced analytics. With that came a switch from case delivery to case management and revenue. A lot of cases in Insights & Research are not that set-up that way. The question then becomes how AAG LT is able to gain visibility in terms of selling. BCG has Insights Partners, while we donâ€™t, and thatâ€™s made it feel like a weird mix. 

Thereâ€™s a big push from Roy [Singh] about selling, and thatâ€™s hard do actually implement because thatâ€™s driven by the practice. Part of the reason we may not get enough work is that weâ€™re more traditional and donâ€™t do flashy things. We have a lot more technical prowess at the top, but it stifles some innovation to do interesting things. You get stuck in a cycle of doing the same types of work. With clients where we have really deep relationships, is there a chance we do the innovative things? That would allow 90%-95% of things to stay the same, while we can try new things.

In some ways, this reshuffling is goodâ€”it puts the researchers together in I&D. My experience at other companies has been that where researchers are spread out, they lose some power. Part of being in research is being able to call out bad ideas and being a center of excellence. I think this will be a net positive. 

Research organizations can be sales-focused. I think thatâ€™s where they wanted to push us, but we didnâ€™t have the Partners to do so. With the move to I&D, we can have centers of excellenceâ€”we might be able to have people dedicated to trainings, for example. We were all generalists, but that ratio of our small team to consultants is never going to work. This may be a good natural inflection point within the team of understanding the goal of Primary Research: is it to invent new SKUs, be innovative, be generalists or specialists? It felt like swimming upstream to terms of finding a niche. Itâ€™s not necessarily a skills mismatch, but Primary Research needs to figure out its mission. 

A lot of people on the Primary Research side enjoy the marketing science and were concerned with the parting with the Insights and Research guild for that reason. They liked working with big data sets, and it was a good match because Insights skewed senior, and Primary Research skewed junior. Thereâ€™s interest among people to be more on the data side, but not sure how feasible that is in terms of joining I&D.

column117:
As a PhD hire, I do not feel that my training and mentorship has been adequate for me to meet the expectations of my tenure. The only difference in training that I received as a PhD hire compared to MBA hires is a 1-week ATP training, which is relatively the same material as Pre-NCT and does not sufficiently provide the on-the-job reps or context needed to succeed. While Bain offers a free pass on your first evaluation (which is intended to be in the first 6 months), this is heavily dependent upon when you enter Bain. In my experiences, I joined in mid-January, staffed on an IP project in mid-February, and received my first evaluation in mid-March when there was less than 4 weeks of actual work experience. I then started my first client case in April as an island role, which was absolutely disastrous given I had about the same level of exposure to Bain as an ACI. I was not sufficiently ready to lead a workstream, nor be evaluated for it. This severely hurt my career trajectory as I had to spend the next review cycle getting up to par, which should have been the focus of my first review cycle.

For comparison, BCG hires PhDs and gives them 4-weeks of ATP training (called a mini-MBA boot camp), followed by 6 months of staffing as a "free extra team resource." This model allows PhD hires to serve in a report-to role to learn the ropes while also providing enough leverage to their team to properly train the PhD hire. While I recommend Bain as a great place to work for culture reasons, I would strongly recommend that PhD hires look towards BCG or McKinsey instead when considering the long-term ramifications of the training and evaluation structure at Bain on a PhD hire's career journey.

column117:
Not on the departure process per se but I do have some feedback regarding integrating senior hires. 
Generally, it felt to me that we only value exclusively Bain experience and Bain methods (toolkit) at the firm, while we may benefit from including experience and techniques that our senior hires have gained elsewhere. It also felt like we integrate senior hires by taking them at one level lower and asking them to take more junior roles until they have "proven themselves" - this is not easy for many people. I think we would have much more success at integrating senior hires if we gave them the freedom to play roles suitable to their level of seniority from the outset - trust that they got to where they are for a reason, trust in our recruitment process and also trust that we have the professional capacities to "save" the situation if it turns out they cannot do it. But asking senior hires to take on junior roles for several cases in a row because they were not bred in Bain can leave a bad taste and hinder them from giving their best performance - many of us operate better when we are trusted.

column117: It's a shame to be leaving a great place. If I could make one suggestion, I would review the impact of certain aspects of the LT on people's careers. At SM and above, there is often an assumption of trust not present with more junior team members, likely as a result of the diligence process and broader LT definition. However, for some individuals hired into LT positions externally, this assumption of trust is still present with no proof points on following the "Bain" approach. I had a particularly difficult case experience with one member of the LT which ultimately resulted in what I felt was a very unfair review and a Bain values flag. Even when I tried to flag this during my case, I was not able to due to the intensity of the LT member's criticism / demands, which utterly annihilated my mental health shortly after losing both my uncle and my father. I had no traction in trying to fight what I thought was unfair, and was shut down at each turn. This is ultimately the reason I am leaving Bain rather than transferring to another office to continue my career here - that one review blocked that opportunity and effectively ended my Bain career. So PLEASE, please, listen with an open mind to your junior and mid level consultants when they raise situations like this - I know mine is not an isolated incident. If we want Bain to continue to be an amazing place to work, we have to protect our values and our culture at all levels, and at all times.

column117: I have a few final thoughts. Being Black at Bain poses a weird challenge that pushes people to be the token and fight for inequities without giving you proper training or guidance to do so. With crazy things happening in the world (like the shooter that killed ten black people and never hearing from my manager or team about how that was insane to them, but they are open to talking about the Chris Rock / Will Smith slap). The people all look and act the same, and if you don't, you're seen as weird, or it affects your career progression. Bain significantly underpays their people, and they expect them to want to stay long-term. As a recruiter at another firm (IB or even McK), the pay is almost 20k more than Bain provides. As a person in business function, hearing that the consulting staff received a 10k raise just because but only providing a 3% increase annually to your business function staff is absurd, especially after cutting down on OT hours but expecting a similar or better output. We hear that Bain's priority is diverse talent, but our recruiting process was riddled with problems to combat biases. Bain talks heavily about wanting to set you up for success when you leave, but I don't feel like anyone was happy about my career change and disliked me for it because we are under so much pressure that one person leaving causes a slew of workstream disalignment. Lastly, and the main reason I have decided to depart, is because I overheard a comment, by a coworker that has continued to not act as a team player, that was extremely transphobic. The worst part is that it was at a dinner with all of our Leadership Team. No one said anything and my current manager even laughed. It may have been a nervous laugh but that made my stomach turn. At that point I knew that it didn't matter what Goldman was offering, Bain was no longer a place that I felt comfortable being. I look forward to talking through all of this at my exit interview.

While I understand the need for prompt transitions for individuals with performance issues and acknowledge that recent growth in the Middle East may have â€œsoftenedâ€ the performance management process, this cycleâ€™s process fundamentally broke the foundations of our performance management system. Key issues include:

1.	Insufficient Communication and Transparency:
o	Several individuals, including those with strong feedback (e.g., SC+ or even FE reviews, as in my case), were transitioned out without prior warnings or feedback about risks to their positions.
o	The process was conducted in a secretive manner, with no effort to inform individuals about the risks involved this cycle.

2.	Overly Top-Down Decision-Making:
o	Decisions were made in a top-down manner, with limited input from leaders directly involved in individualsâ€™ day-to-day work.
o	This led to inconsistencies between decisions and feedback received, creating confusion and a sense of unfairness. For instance, some individuals with promotion recommendations from their LT and sponsors were still let go.

3.	Exclusion of PD Advisors:
o	PD advisors were excluded from Talent Committee discussions in many cases. For example, I was removed from the TC for a C5 I supported. This undermined the integrity of the process and led to decisions not fully grounded in performance evidence.

4.	Lack of Improvement Pathways or Alternatives:
o	For individuals with performance concerns, PIPs were not provided as a path for improvement, deviating from Bainâ€™s standard practices. 
o	Alternative pathways (e.g., unpaid leaves or reallocations) were not offered, unlike in other offices.

I strongly believe this process undermines Bainâ€™s implicit contract with employees, which is built on fairness, transparency, and rigor. If left unaddressed, it risks negatively impacting employee trust, retention, and Bainâ€™s reputation as a meritocratic and â€œTrue Northâ€ organization.

I was a proud advocate for Bain and believed deeply in the firm's values. But I now leave feeling like I was treated as part of a rushed corporate layoff, without genuine care or consideration I expected from Bain.
